opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's an interesting question, because in some ways large language models look like the triumph of the bitter lesson. They're using massive computation, they scale, and they've largely set aside the hand-engineered linguistic knowledge that people used to build in. So people say, "Look, Rich, this is your lesson, vindicated."

But I think it's more mixed than that. The bitter lesson is really about methods that scale with computation and that learn from experience, rather than relying on what we humans put in. And large language models learn mostly from human-generated text. They're mimicking what people say. That's a huge store of human knowledge, and when that runs out, or when you need something beyond what people have already written down, there's no obvious way for the system to keep improving.

What's missing is learning from experience: an agent that acts in the world, sees what happens, and gets some notion of reward, of what's good or bad. That's where you have a ground truth. A language model predicts the next token, but it doesn't have a goal in the world, and it isn't surprised by what actually happens in a way that lets it update its understanding. It's predicting what a person would say, not what will happen.

So I'd say large language models are partly an example of the bitter lesson and partly an example of its opposite. They lean heavily on human knowledge. Historically, the approaches that lean on human knowledge do well for a while, and then they get overtaken by methods that learn directly from experience and scale better. I expect that's what will happen here too. The systems that eventually supersede LLMs will be ones that learn from experience on their own. When that happens, it'll be another instance of the bitter lesson: we built in the human knowledge, it felt good, and then something more general came along and did better.

r001.rationale: The response says human-generated text may run out, but does not identify Internet training data as the limit on scaling through more computation.

r002.rationale: It describes LLMs as learning from human-generated text and calls that text a huge store of human knowledge.

r003.rationale: It expects systems that learn from experience on their own to eventually supersede LLMs.

r004.rationale: It calls that supersession another instance of the bitter lesson: built-in human knowledge is overtaken by a more general approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think people see large language models as a vindication of the bitter lesson, and I'd actually push back on that. The bitter lesson is about scalable methods, methods that get better as you give them more computation. And on the surface, LLMs look like that. They use enormous compute, they learn from data rather than from hand-coded rules, and they keep improving with scale. So in that narrow sense, sure, they fit.

But I think they're also a bit of a trap, and it's the same trap we've fallen into before. What they're really doing is learning to imitate people. They're trained to predict the next token in text that humans wrote. That's a form of putting human knowledge into the system. It's a more sophisticated form than writing down rules, but it's still leaning on us, on what people happen to have said and thought. And the lesson of the last seventy years is that leaning on human knowledge works for a while, and then it plateaus, and the methods that just learn from experience go past it.

What an LLM doesn't have is a goal. It doesn't have a sense of what it's trying to achieve in the world, and so it doesn't have any ground truth about whether it's right. When you predict the next word, there's no right answer in the world, only what some person said. Contrast that with an agent that acts, sees what happens, and gets a reward. That agent can be surprised. It can be wrong and find out. That's the beginning of real learning, and it's what I'd call learning from experience rather than learning from people.

So my view is that LLMs are impressive, I don't want to be dismissive, but they're a detour. They're a way of getting a lot of mileage out of the human record. And I'd expect that eventually, what we'll find is that the systems which learn continually, from their own interaction with the world, from their own goals, will go further. The internet is finite. Experience isn't. And I think that's the version of the bitter lesson that's still ahead of us, not behind us.

r001.rationale: The response says the internet is finite, but does not clearly identify the limited supply of internet training data as a constraint on scaling LLMs with more computation.

r002.rationale: It says LLMs imitate people by predicting tokens in human-written text and describes this as putting human knowledge into the system.

r003.rationale: It expects systems learning continually from their own interaction and goals to go further than LLMs relying on the human record.

r004.rationale: It calls that future shift to systems learning from experience the version of the bitter lesson still ahead.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re partly an illustration of the bitter lesson. You have a fairly general method, you give it enormous amounts of computation and data, and it does much better than systems where people tried to put in their understanding of language. You don’t build in a grammar or a theory of how people reason. You learn. That’s very much in the spirit of the bitter lesson.

But I wouldn’t interpret that as saying that large language models, as we have them now, are the final answer. The bitter lesson is about methods that can continue to scale, particularly learning and search. And learning from a fixed collection of human-written text has a limitation: the supply of that experience comes from us.

What I’m interested in is an agent that learns from its own experience. It takes actions, sees what happens, and learns to do better. It can discover things that nobody has written down, and it can keep learning as the world changes.

So I would distinguish the success of the general approach from the particular source of training data. The success of large language models is significant. But the broader opportunity is learning from interaction with the world, where the experience available to the system can grow along with its ability to generate and learn from it.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed human-written text limits available experience, but does not identify Internet training data or explicitly connect that limit to scaling through more computation.

r002.rationale: It describes LLMs as learning from a fixed collection of human-written text, clearly identifying human-produced material as their training source.

r003.rationale: It presents learning from interaction as a broader opportunity, but does not say or clearly predict that such systems could outperform LLMs trained on human-produced data.

r004.rationale: The response calls current LLMs partly an illustration of the bitter lesson, but does not say that experience-learning systems may supersede them as an instance of that lesson.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re largely an example of the bitter lesson. Instead of trying to build our knowledge of language into a system—our grammatical rules, our theories of how meaning works—we use a relatively general learning method and a tremendous amount of computation. And that turns out to work much better than the approaches where people tried to put in more of their own understanding.

But I wouldn’t conclude that predicting the next word is the whole answer to intelligence. These systems learn from enormous amounts of human-produced text. That’s a powerful source of experience, but we also want agents that can act in the world, see the consequences of their actions, and keep learning. They need to discover how to achieve goals through their own experience.

So I see language models as a success for the general approach, while leaving open the question of what the learning system ultimately should be. The bitter lesson doesn’t say that whatever method is successful today is the final method. It says we should favor methods that can continue to improve as we give them more computation and more experience.

r001.rationale: The response mentions enormous amounts of human-produced text but does not identify the supply of Internet data as a limit on scaling through more computation.

r002.rationale: It says language models learn from human-produced text, but describes that text as a source of experience rather than characterizing the training as incorporating human knowledge.

r003.rationale: The response says agents should learn through their own experience, but does not express an expectation that they could outperform language models trained on human-produced data.

r004.rationale: It leaves open what learning system will ultimately work and favors methods that improve with computation and experience, but does not identify supersession of human-knowledge-based language models as an instance of the bitter lesson.
